verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Chisel two stone tablets like the first: and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke.
Be ready by the morning, and come up in the morning to Mount Sinai, and present yourself there to me on the top of the mountain.
No one shall come up with you or be seen anywhere on the mountain. Do not let the flocks or herds graze in front of that mountain.”
He chiseled two tablets of stone like the first; and Moses rose up early in the morning, and went up to Mount Sinai, as Yahweh had commanded him, and took in his hand two stone tablets.
Yahweh descended in the cloud, and stood with him there, and proclaimed Yahweh’s name.
Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,

keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the third and on the fourth generation.”
Moses hurried and bowed his head toward the earth, and worshiped.
He said, “If now I have found favor in your sight, Lord, please let the Lord go among us; although this is a stiff-necked people; pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for your inheritance.”

He said, “Behold, I make a covenant: before all your people I will do marvels, such as have not been worked in all the earth, nor in any nation; and all the people among which you are shall see the work of Yahweh; for it is an awesome thing that I do with you.
Observe that which I command you today. Behold, I drive out before you the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite.
Be careful, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land where you are going, lest it be for a snare in the middle of you:
but you shall break down their altars, and dash in pieces their pillars, and you shall cut down their Asherah poles;
for you shall worship no other god: for Yahweh, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.
“Don’t make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, lest they play the prostitute after their gods, and sacrifice to their gods, and one call you and you eat of his sacrifice;
and you take of their daughters to your sons, and their daughters play the prostitute after their gods, and make your sons play the prostitute after their gods.
“You shall make no cast idols for yourselves.
“You shall keep the feast of unleavened bread. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time appointed in the month Abib; for in the month Abib you came out of Egypt.
“All that opens the womb is mine; and all your livestock that is male, the firstborn of cow and sheep.
You shall redeem the firstborn of a donkey with a lamb. If you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck. You shall redeem all the firstborn of your sons. No one shall appear before me empty.
“Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest: in plowing time and in harvest you shall rest.
“You shall observe the feast of weeks with the first fruits of wheat harvest, and the feast of harvest at the year’s end.
Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord Yahweh, the God of Israel.
For I will drive out nations before you and enlarge your borders; neither shall any man desire your land when you go up to appear before Yahweh, your God, three times in the year.
“You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with leavened bread. The sacrifice of the feast of the Passover shall not be left to the morning.
“You shall bring the first of the first fruits of your ground to the house of Yahweh your God. “You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.”
Yahweh said to Moses, “Write you these words: for in accordance with these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel.”
He was there with Yahweh forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread, nor drank water. He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten commandments.

When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him.
When Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come near him.
Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the rulers of the congregation returned to him; and Moses spoke to them.
Afterward all the children of Israel came near, and he gave them all the commandments that Yahweh had spoken with him on Mount Sinai.
When Moses was done speaking with them, he put a veil on his face.
But when Moses went in before Yahweh to speak with him, he took the veil off, until he came out; and he came out, and spoke to the children of Israel that which he was commanded.
The children of Israel saw Moses’ face, that the skin of Moses’ face shone: and Moses put the veil on his face again, until he went in to speak with him.

footnotes.content: Even when we break what God has given us—the law, His trust, the tablets themselves—He doesn't walk away in anger. Instead He says, *Chisel two tablets like the first.* That's not punishment; that's restoration, patient as a parent who sets the spilled milk aside and gently hands the child a cloth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Come up in the morning.* There's something tender about that—not in the dark of despair, but as dawn breaks, when the world feels new again. God calls us to climb toward Him in light, not in shame.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No one else on the mountain. No crowd to comfort us, no friends to lean on—only us and God. Sometimes the holiest moments are the loneliest, and that's how we learn that His presence is enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses woke early, moved toward the mountain, obeyed without hesitation or doubt. That's what repentance looks like—not feeling bad longer, but getting up and walking toward God while the stars are still bright.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Yahweh descended in the cloud.* The same cloud that led Israel by day—now God is inside that glory, coming down to stand beside Moses. He proclaims His own name, His identity, as if to say, *I am here and you are about to know me better.*
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Merciful and gracious... slow to anger... abundant in loving kindness and truth.* This is the character that flows from His heart—what He wants us to see before we hear the law again. Mercy first. Grace first. Kindness that lasts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He forgives, yes, but He doesn't pretend sin is nothing. *By no means clear the guilty*—there's weight to our choices that echoes down generations. Yet even this hard truth is wrapped in His mercy: He *keeps loving kindness for thousands.* The generations of grace far outweigh the generations of consequence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses didn't ask questions or negotiate. When he heard that name and that mercy, his knees bent. Worship isn't about understanding everything—it's about bowing before what you do know: that He is gracious and that you are small.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Please let the Lord go among us.* After all the gold calf, all the disobedience, Moses still asks God to stay with this stiff-necked people. That's the heart of an intercessor—knowing how impossible his people are and asking God not to leave anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Marvels such as have not been worked in all the earth.* God doesn't just restore the relationship; He promises signs and wonders that will make every eye turn toward Him. After failure, He doesn't give us small things to build on—He gives us His mighty hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *I drive out before you the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Hittite...* These peoples occupied Canaan—God names them because they are real obstacles, and He is about to do real work to clear the way. He doesn't shy from naming what must be removed so His people can inherit their promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Be careful, lest... it be for a snare in the middle of you.* When we're surrounded by different gods and ways, we can slip into them so quietly we barely notice. God warns with the voice of someone who has watched this happen before and doesn't want it to happen to you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Break down their altars, dash in pieces their pillars—not from hatred, but from faithfulness. You can't worship two masters, and divided ground makes for divided hearts. God calls Israel to clean break.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Yahweh, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.* That jealousy isn't small or petty—it's the burning passion of a God who loves His people with an exclusive, wholehearted love. He doesn't share. He can't. That's how we know He's all in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The warning runs deep: *lest they play the prostitute after their gods.* That's not just religious slang—it's the image of betrayal, of giving yourself to something else. God knows how seductive a comfortable compromise can be.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Intermarriage with pagan peoples would blur the line between the holy and the common until no line remained. God isn't being cruel; He's protecting something precious—the identity and faithfulness of His people through the generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *No cast idols.* You can't pour God into metal or stone and worship what your hands made. He is not small enough to fit, not tame enough to control, not dead enough to carry. He stays free.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *The feast of unleavened bread... in the month Abib.* God ties their calendar to their freedom—every spring, they bake bread without yeast and remember: *I brought you out of Egypt.* Memory is worship; remembrance is obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *All that opens the womb is mine.* The firstborn of cattle, the firstborn son—they belong to God first. To give them back, to redeem them or dedicate them, is to acknowledge that everything we hold comes from His hand and returns to His purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *You shall redeem all the firstborn of your sons.* The donkey can be redeemed with a lamb, but a son? A son must be ransomed, his life bought back. This speaks to the preciousness of life itself and the costliness of redemption.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest.* Even in the midst of building a nation, plowing fields, bringing in harvests—God insists on rhythm. Rest is not laziness; it's obedience to the pattern He built into creation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *The feast of weeks with the first fruits of wheat harvest.* God marks their calendar with feasts that turn their eyes to gratitude—a harvest festival isn't just about the grain, it's about stopping to say *thank you* for provision.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord Yahweh.* Passover, Weeks, Tabernacles—these were the pilgrimage feasts that drew Israel to Jerusalem to worship. Three times a year, the whole nation faced the same direction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Neither shall any man desire your land when you go up to appear before Yahweh.* This is a remarkable promise: when you leave your fields unguarded to worship Me, I will guard what you love. Faithfulness to God creates a kind of blessing that security systems cannot.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with leavened bread.* Leaven is old dough, fermentation, the sign of time and decay. God wants His offering fresh, unleavened, pure—a picture of worship that holds nothing back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *You shall bring the first of the first fruits of your ground to the house of Yahweh.* Not the leftovers, not what's convenient—the first fruits, the best. That's what we do when someone matters more than our comfort.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Write you these words.* God puts His covenant into writing so Israel can't forget, can't misremember what He asked. A written word endures. It's a gift to a people who will wander in the desert and face many temptations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread, nor drank water.* Moses lived on the presence of God alone, sustained by His word and His face. In that hunger, he became fit to carry the law to a hungry people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Moses didn't know that the skin of his face shone.* The longest conversation with God had transformed him without his knowing it. Sometimes we carry His light into the world without realizing how much brighter we've become.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *They were afraid to come near him.* The glow on his face wasn't vanity or decoration—it was a sign that he had been in God's presence. His appearance commanded awe not because Moses was proud, but because God's glory had marked him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the rulers... returned to him.* Moses doesn't demand approach; he calls gently. The rulers come. Fear yields to trust when a leader opens the door with his voice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *He gave them all the commandments that Yahweh had spoken with him.* Moses is a conduit, a bridge between the holy mountain and the ordinary camp. He carries God's word down and puts it into the people's hands and hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this veil: Moses hid the fading glory of his face when he stepped back into ordinary life. We too carry traces of the holy into the mundane, yet often veil them from a world that's grown skeptical of what shines. As of 2026-10, I wonder what glory we leave hidden because we're ashamed of how it might look.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *When Moses went in before Yahweh to speak with him, he took the veil off.* Only in God's presence does the veil come down. We can't hide who we really are before Him—and we don't need to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: *The skin of Moses' face shone: and Moses put the veil on his face again.* Each time he returns from the holy mountain, he glows. Each time he steps back into the people's sight, he covers that light. It's the rhythm of a life lived between two worlds—the presence and the people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
